data.title: Peter Schreiber: the “second life” of prehistoric stone industry
data.excerpt: Prehistoric stone arrowheads turn up in the graves of the early medieval Merovingian period, and Western scholarship reads them as amulets against demonic forces. The archaeologist Peter Schreiber follows this second life of prehistoric stone tools from medieval superstition as far as the 19th century.

data.metaDescription: Why prehistoric stone arrowheads appear in early medieval graves – read as amulets against demons. A text by the archaeologist Peter Schreiber.

children.text: Western archaeological literature has so far interpreted finds of older, prehistoric arrowheads

in the grave inventories of the early medieval Merovingian period only sparingly and without closer detail, as amulets which people wore while still alive. These objects were regarded as a defence against so-called demonic forces

, and their primary function was probably that of a talisman. The magical properties attributed to them have their roots even before the medieval period, and in the course of that period they developed further (Reisch 2005). These finds are, however, difficult to interpret today – that is, to tell whether they really are stone tools from prehistory – because they survive only in fragments. They may be confused with contemporary medieval strike-a-light stones, which were used together with a metal fire-steel to kindle a fire.
In medieval superstition, magical effects were generally attributed to silicites (rocks containing silica which flake readily
). For the Anglo-Saxons, for example, the sparks were a means of protection against lightning, thunder and floods, and according to Saxo Grammaticus also “against the working of demons”.

In later periods, finds of prehistoric arrowheads were generally regarded in the traditions of Western Europe and in the Mediterranean region as objects with supernatural, protective and healing powers. Flint arrowheads, so-called “thunderstones”, were linked in popular belief with storms. From Italy, for example, there are known superstitions that stone points made of chert protected against storms.

children.text: In the Slavic world their counterpart are polished Neolithic and Eneolithic axes, or axe-hammers, which were hung on the fronts of dwellings as protection against lightning.

were still being carried in the 19th century as a talisman, an object protecting against bad weather. They were carried in the pocket or on the hat. They were also placed beneath the windows of stables in order to “protect” the cattle from disease. These notions are also attested in an area reaching from the Balkans and Greece as far as Africa. In the British Isles and in Scandinavia the flint points were called “elf arrows” and were credited with protective as well as healing powers (Reisch 2005).
